# 14-code-four — sources

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

whys.g1: Both answers describe the person who signs off waiting on another office first, the DA or the neighboring sheriff, which I'd recognise as the same hold-up, and the group name says so plainly.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; both answers are on-topic replies about who has to agree.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: One answer says a pilot proving faster reports would justify paying more and the other says report writing costs nothing extra to justify spending at all, so they are different positions and leaving each on its own with no group to misplace them in is how I would sort them.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line, since both answers speak directly to price and value, so it stays at the default of 2.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and launch, but the buyer's cost and price (screens 12-13) come before who else must agree and what could stop a purchase (screens 14-18), when I'd rather describe how a department buys, chief's cap and council, before naming a price that depends on that cap.
founder.missing: Nothing asks whether the department's records system and body-cam vendor will work with the product, or whether the footage can be accessed at all; Axon owns many departments' cameras and evidence storage and also sells Draft One, so that dependency and the head-to-head with an incumbent tool should be asked directly rather than left to surface in free-text friction. Nothing asks about CJIS compliance or evidence-handling rules either, which a chief will ask about first.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes in a sensible sequence from whether my department qualifies, to the idea, to the hours we spend now, then value, funding, sign-off, the trial and finally a pilot.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing asked whether the reports would hold up with the DA and in court, or how the tool handles CJIS security, footage storage and integration with our records management system; those would decide this for me as much as price.

screens.why5: The hours and base are mine, but "Police chiefs already spend 40 to 60 hours per officer a month" is wrong because officers spend those hours and the department pays for them.
screens.instead: What do incident reports cost the department today? Options: Money it spends / Officer hours it pays for / A share of revenue or budget it loses; chip: I'm not sure -- belief line: "Incident reports already cost the department 40 to 60 officer hours per officer a month."

screens.why1: Right after what the problem costs the department, it is obvious to ask what price I have in mind, and the belief about chiefs follows from it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but "A percent of the incident reports" takes a second read because nobody in police software prices that way, and "what it gets back" is vague to me.
screens.why3: I set the price, so I can answer at once: a monthly subscription at $30 per officer.
screens.why4: My fixed monthly fee per officer is there, the "No price yet" chip fits and the set is complete, but the percent options are odd for a department buying report software, since a report has no dollar value to take a percent of and nothing is "got back".
screens.why5: The belief line says police chiefs would think it worth $30 per officer a month, which is my price, my unit and my buyer.
screens.instead: What price do you have in mind for something that cuts the paperwork after a call? Options: A fixed fee per officer each month; A fixed fee for the whole department each year; A fee per report; One price, then a fee each month; One price, then nothing more; Free to them. Chip: No price yet.

screens.why1: Right after who decides and the price, it is obvious to ask who else has to sign off before a department can buy.
screens.why2: Chief, agree and buy are how I talk about a department sale, and I can answer on first reading with the council or city manager.
screens.why3: I sell to chiefs and know from those conversations who else can stop a purchase, including the council above the spending cap.
screens.why4: The free-text box lets me name the council and city manager, the hint makes 'Nobody' a valid answer, and the escape chip suits a founder who would rather not test this.
screens.why5: Keel keeps my chief as buyer, but 'nobody else has to agree' drops the spending cap that makes the chief's sign-off enough at $30 an officer, and it sits oddly beside the council and city manager I typed.
screens.instead: Besides the police chief, who has to agree before they can buy at this price? (e.g. the city council, if it is over the chief's spending limit; "Nobody" is an answer)

screens.why1: Right after I named who else has to agree, it makes sense to check the list of people Keel will use before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The words are all mine (patrol officer, chief, city council, city manager), but I need a second read to see why the council and manager are listed with no label when the belief says nobody else has to agree.
screens.why3: I sell to these departments and know who has the problem, who signs and who can get in the way, as I saw with Heber City's chief and council.
screens.why4: The people are complete and distinct, and the officer-versus-chief split is right, but the two bare rows don't say whether they are people who might have to agree or who sign above the cap, and "patrol officer" and "Police chief" are capitalised differently.
screens.why5: The roles are kept and nothing was added, but "nobody else has to agree" drops the spending cap: the chief decides alone only under it, and the council decides above it.
screens.instead: Keep the rows but label the last two: patrol officer · has the problem; police chief · decides to buy, within their spending limit; city council · might have to agree; city manager · might have to agree; with the belief reading "At this price, the police chief can decide alone; we're testing whether anyone else has to agree."

screens.why1: Right after I named the council and city manager as possible approvers, it makes sense to choose the single sign-off belief to test with chiefs.
screens.why2: The roles are plain to me, but 'Pick the one role; nothing is reworded here' needs a second read, and 'Nobody else' is not a role.
screens.why3: Who signs off when a department buys software is something I learn directly from selling to chiefs, so I can choose from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and in my words, but none captures the spending cap, where the chief decides alone below it and the council must approve above it, so 'Nobody else' is the closest fit rather than the exact answer.
screens.why5: 'The police chief decides, and nobody else has to agree' keeps my picked answer but drops the condition that this holds only under the chief's spending cap, which is why our price clears when Draft One's does not.
screens.instead: Which belief do you want to test? The chief can approve this alone because it is under their spending cap / The city council has to agree / The city manager has to agree.

screens.why1: Right after settling who signs off, it makes sense to ask what could stall the sale, and I know this from every department I've pitched.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me, but the belief's tail, "or not need it," took a second read to see it means chiefs who would skip the trial.
screens.why3: I live these stalls every week: bake-offs against Draft One, RMS fit, and DAs who hesitate over AI-drafted reports.
screens.why4: The only option is the free-text box and its escape chip, and my three items fit the box while "Leave this out of the study" is a fair way out for a step not every founder needs.
screens.why5: The Axon trial is kept, but the belief adds an 8-week limit I never typed and drops the records-system check and the prosecutor's agreement without saying so.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase? (Approvals, reviews, procurement, switching.) Belief: Most police chiefs could finish a side-by-side trial against Axon's tool within about 8 weeks, and some wouldn't need a trial at all.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it is obvious why Keel asks me to pick the one step to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: Trial, records system, prosecutor's office and budget approval are all my trade's words, but "if they bought it, how long would this step take before it went through" needs a second read because a trial comes before the purchase and doesn't "go through".
screens.why3: I sell to chiefs and know these trials run 30 days against Axon and then a decision, so about 8 weeks is an estimate I can make from my own work.
screens.why4: The four steps are distinct, are the real hold-ups in a department purchase and are in the words chiefs use, and days, weeks and months cover any answer.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my pick and my 8 weeks, and "or not need it" fairly counts chiefs who would buy without a trial.
screens.instead: Intro: The person who decides gets one question for this: how long would this step take them before they could buy? Pick the one step.

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs, the price and what slows a purchase, asking what first step I want from the chief is the obvious last commercial question, and a free pilot is how I actually sell.
screens.why2: "First real step" and the hint are plain to me, but "them" could mean the chief, the officers or the strangers named on the last screen, and only the belief line shows it means the chief.
screens.why3: Getting departments into a no-strings pilot is what I do every week, so I can answer this straight from how I sell.
screens.why4: The box takes my own words with room for the answer, the hint's time, data, money or signature covers a pilot's real cost, and leaving it out is a fitting escape.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my "run a free pilot with a few officers" and correctly puts it on the police chief, the "in most cases" and "now" being only Keel's framing of the claim.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the police chief to take? Something that costs the department time, data, money or a signature. Up to 25 words.

screens.why1: Straight after I typed the first step I want from a chief, it makes sense for Keel to show me how that step will be tested before the commercial section closes.
screens.why2: "Under 9 words" and "as strangers hear it" take a second read, because the only sentence shown runs 16 words and I have to work out that the limit applies to just "run a free pilot with a few officers".
screens.why3: Free pilots with chiefs are how I sell, so I know straight away whether a chief would run one now.
screens.why4: The only thing to settle is the wording of the step, and it is complete and in my words, while the bar's "probably not or no" is a clear, fair line for a free pilot.
screens.why5: It keeps my offer of a free, no-strings pilot with a few officers, the chief is the right decider, and "now" fits my 48-hour setup.
screens.instead: Your step as police chiefs will hear it, kept under 9 words: "run a free pilot with a few officers".

screens.why1: I just named a free pilot as my first real step, so asking whether to offer it before the study goes out is an obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" is plain to me, but I had to reread "people who say yes get a line" because it doesn't say what they said yes to, and I haven't seen the "Pilot tab".
screens.why3: Offering free pilots to departments is how I sell, so I can answer this at once from what I already do.
screens.why4: Yes and no are the only two choices here, they are distinct and clear, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The line shown to people drops the "free" and "a few officers" from my step, and it doesn't say whether a patrol officer's email gets a pilot when the chief is the one who decides.
screens.instead: Offer your free pilot with a few officers? People who finish the study see: "Would you try a free pilot with a few officers? Leave your email." You'll see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, it makes obvious sense to settle who will put the questions to my patrol officers.
screens.why2: It reads clearly and 'patrol officers' is my word, but the hint packs in video, typing, recording, credits and text-message delivery, and 'Keel records the voice you pick once' takes a second read when what is being locked is a face and voice.
screens.why3: Picking an interviewer after hearing a five-second sample needs no outside knowledge, and I can judge which one my officers would sit through.
screens.why4: Two distinct, named interviewers with a sample to hear, a preselected default and a flat price are all the choice needs, and no escape chip is required because the hint offers typing or tapping for respondents.
screens.why5: It keeps 'patrol officers' exactly as I typed it and changes nothing about my idea, buyer or price.
screens.instead: Who should ask patrol officers your questions? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to hear her and switch. Your choice is recorded once for this project: 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks patrol officers the questions, it makes obvious sense to choose separately how the chiefs, who are the buyers, will answer, right before sending.
screens.why2: The question and options are easy to follow, but "Daphne" needs a moment to register as the AI interviewer's name, and the leftover labels "Hear her" and "Still recording" run into the text and take a second read.
screens.why3: I know how chiefs work, at a desk between calls and meetings, and can judge whether they would rather tap through a short form or talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct and the true answer is there, but "Ready when Daphne is" and "Still recording" are odd status wording that makes me work out what waits on what.
screens.why5: It correctly keeps my buyer as the chief, separate from the patrol officers, and changes nothing I typed about the study.
screens.instead: How should chiefs answer? AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud on video and each question is also on screen; ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready in a few minutes).

screens.why1: Right after choosing how chiefs answer, the last thing to settle before sending is who receives a link, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: The question and first option are plain to me, but 'People I found with Keel' and 'the Contacts page' name a tool feature I need the description to understand, and I have to work out whether 'who gets a link' means officers, chiefs or both.
screens.why3: I know how I reach people: chiefs and officers I have been introduced to, whom I can name and write to one at a time.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the open link's Google sign-in fits department people poorly and there is no way to say I want one route for named chiefs and another for officers posted to a group.
screens.why5: It adds nothing to my idea and does not change it, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as I gave it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link for this study of patrol officers and chiefs? People I know by name (I send each their own link) / A list I find with Keel (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google first).

screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment are word for word what I checked, but Existing sacrifice says police chiefs spend 40 to 60 hours per officer on reports, when my officers spend those hours, not their chiefs.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Code Four or what to do about the trial against Axon or the 3 chiefs who can't sign alone; the only sentence of explanation just says who was asked.

screens.why_b5: It shows 8 answered and 7 counted, explains Patricia's 0 and Gerald's exclusion, says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and claims nothing beyond these chiefs.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "5 of 7 at $30 or more per officer a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I have both the answer and the number that decides it, and they agree.

screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to the Ability to pay card, but it never says what this means for my $30, such as keeping the price while treating it as unproven with only one chief to spare.
screens.why_b5: The count stays visible and "a small group: a lean, not a call" is honest, but the So line turns an answer about what Code Four would be worth into "would pay", which is a soft overstatement from 7 chiefs who have not committed any money.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside the deciding count, 4 of 5 from money already there against a bar of 4 of 5, and it says that is exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see four budget sources counted over 5 chiefs, each marked for or against, with the bar marked at 4 of 5 and the strip showing 4 for and 1 against.
screens.why_b3: The $30 per officer a month and the chiefs are mine, but this budget line is not among the beliefs I checked on the way in, so I recognise it rather than remember it.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to expect the money from chiefs who named my price and sends me to the next card on who has to agree, which is my real question given the spending cap and the council.
screens.why_b5: The n of 5, the three chiefs not asked and "a lean, not a call" are all visible, but "Expect the money to be there for the 5" overstates it because Marcus would need a new line and counts against.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right above "5 of 8 could sign alone · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short", so I have the answer and the deciding number together, even though the line above the count names only two of the three against.

screens.why_b2: The bands, the 8 people and the for and against counts are plain, but the bar needs a second look because the verdict says no more than 2 of 8 against while the chart says 6 of 8 and marks the strip at 6.

Answers tie at 3 for 1 month to under 8 weeks and 3 for 8 weeks to 6 months, and 2 need no trial, so plan for 8 weeks but allow for some chiefs taking longer; what would take the time is on the Insights tab.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so the verdict and the number that decides it agree.
screens.why_b2: The three bars (6 yes, 1 probably not, 1 no), the 8 people and the marker at 6 of 8 are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The name Commitment and the line about the chief running a free pilot with a few officers are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is the right concrete move for me, because the six named chiefs who said yes can go straight into pilots.
screens.why_b5: The n of 8 stays visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", the at-the-bar result is not called strong, and the question is shown as hypothetical ("if it were offered today").

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its status word with the deciding number beside it, such as Purchase friction: Did not hold, 3 of 8 expect longer than 8 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b3: The three names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, including my Axon trial and the chief deciding alone, and the Price line says my $30 per officer a month.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these results mean for the idea, so I have to work out for myself that I should bring the DA, council and neighbouring agencies in early, and Purchase friction gives me nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay visible and the three people who never saw the Purchase friction question are named, but 'the 2 who said no' overstates Ingrid, who would pay $10 to under $30, and nothing says that two quotes from 7 or 8 chiefs are thin.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: the city manager wants the DA's view first, the council is watching the sheriff next door, one chief wants pilot proof of faster reports through review, and another sees report time as already paid for, though the 'On their own' label adds nothing and Purchase friction has no quotes.
screens.instead: Buyer and payer: both chiefs who explained were waiting on someone outside the department, the DA or the sheriff next door, so line up that outside view before asking for a signature; Purchase friction: nobody was asked why, so ask Marcus, Tomas and Gerald what would take the time; Price: of the 2 under $30, one would pay less until a pilot proves it and one would pay nothing because report time is already paid for.

screens.why1: A first question about department size makes obvious sense as a screener for a study about police work.
screens.why2: "Department" and "officers" are how I talk every day, and I can answer the moment I hear it.
screens.why3: I'm the chief, so I know my headcount exactly, and it isn't something I'd have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a screener with a clear range, and no escape chip is needed because any chief knows the answer.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 10 to 200 officer range and shows nothing of a product or the founder's terms, though it drops the police, sheriff, transit and university detail without changing the meaning.
screens.why6: It is one short question with numbers that say easily, and yes or no is simple to hold after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After confirming my department's size, and under a heading about the buying decision, it makes sense to show me the product before asking what I'd do about it.
screens.why2: Body-cam footage, narrative report, records format and redaction are all my language, but "a drafted narrative report" is an odd way to say what a product is and I'd need a second read of "check words they must catch."
screens.why3: My officers write these reports from body-cam calls and I review and pay for the tools, so I can weigh this from what I know.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: Reading it as the idea on purpose is fine, but "a drafted narrative report" names an output instead of a tool, and the benefit line says "you review and sign" when the card says officers do, so the meaning has drifted between chief and officer.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences, but it is a lot to hold on one hearing, and "with check words they must catch" and "redacts footage in one click and searches it" are mouthfuls that don't explain themselves when heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts narrative reports from body-cam footage. Your officers upload a call's footage, and it drafts the report in your records format, ties each fact to its clip and plants check words they must catch before they sign. It also redacts footage in one click and searches it. The people building it believe your officers would review and sign instead of writing from scratch.

screens.why1: Right after an idea about report writing, it makes sense to ask what those reports cost my department in time today before talking about buying anything.
screens.why2: I know what an incident report is, but 'hours per officer' makes me stop and work out an average, and 'the incident reports' sounds like a specific set nobody has named yet.
screens.why3: As chief I can pull report counts and have a feel for how long they take, but we don't track report-writing hours per officer, so my number would be an informed guess.
screens.why4: A number box fits, and 'None' and 'I can't recall' are distinct and cover the other honest answers, though no department of mine would truly say none.
screens.why5: It asks only about time my department spends on reports, without naming the product or using any founder language.
screens.why6: The question itself says fine, but 'hours per officer last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clumsy instruction to take in by ear once.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many hours did a typical officer in your department spend writing incident reports? A number of hours, or a low and a high. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours question, asking what it is worth to me per officer is the obvious next thing for the chief who pays for it.
screens.why2: Per officer, per month is exactly how we budget and get quoted for Axon and records software, so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I buy software on per-officer pricing inside a spending cap, so I can put a real number on this from what I already pay.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover the range from pocket change to a serious add-on, and both 'I wouldn't pay for this' and 'I can't say' fit.
screens.why5: No roles or plans leak, but 'a drafted narrative report' is a thin, odd description of a product and 'worth to you' drifts slightly from what the thing would actually cost me.
screens.why6: It says well and the two steps are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' is a clumsy mouthful and 'to under' trips a little when heard.

screens.why1: Right after I give a price, it makes sense to ask where that money would come from, because that's the next thing I'd have to work out as chief.
screens.why2: I deal with budget lines every year, so I can answer this on first read.
screens.why3: I build and defend the department's budget, so I know whether this would come from an existing line, a new request or a cut elsewhere.
screens.why4: Grant money is how a department like mine often pays for this kind of tool and it has no clear option, and the past-tense wording of 'someone signed off' and 'there was no budget' doesn't fit a hypothetical purchase.
screens.why5: It's a plain budget question about the price I gave, and nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaks through.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four options I can hold, but 'a new budget line someone signed off' is a clumsy mouthful and 'Or say you can't say' sounds awkward aloud.
screens.instead: If you went ahead at that price, where would the money come from? A budget line you already have; a new budget line; a grant; taken from other spending; or there'd be no budget for it. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after asking where the money would come from, it makes sense to ask whether I can approve the spend or need the city manager or council to agree.
screens.why2: "Sign off" is how I talk about purchases, so I can answer this on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my spending authority is and when a purchase has to go to the city manager or council.
screens.why4: "I can't recall one" makes no sense here because there is no "one" to recall, and the three "No" options overlap, with the "Yes" oddly placed after the first of them.
screens.why5: No product or founder language leaks, but I said about $30 to $50 and it has quietly become about $30, which is an easier amount to approve.
screens.why6: It is one question and I could follow it, but three similar "no" options are hard to hold after one hearing, and "say you can't recall one" would leave me wondering what "one" means.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $30 to $50 per officer a month yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself; No, one other person would have to agree; No, several people would have to agree; No, someone else would decide. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and trial time, asking whether I'd actually run a pilot is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: Running a pilot with a few officers is how a chief talks about trying new software, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Deciding whether to put a new tool in front of a few officers is my call, and I can answer it from how I run the department.
screens.why4: The options are clear and cover the answer, but there is a firm yes, a soft no and a hard no with no matching 'probably yes', and I'd likely want to say yes only if it clears city and records review.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, but 'a drafted narrative report' is an odd way to describe Code Four, since it names the output rather than a tool that drafts it from body-cam footage.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, with three options I can hold after hearing it once, and the shift to 'you'd' reads naturally aloud.
